metadata.file_name: 30. Wang et al. (2023). Understanding Students’ Subjective and Eudaimonic Well‑Being: Combining both Machine Learning and Classical Statistics.pdf
metadata.title: Understanding Students’ Subjective and Eudaimonic Well‑Being: Combining both Machine Learning and Classical Statistics

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses publicly available PISA 2018 microdata for Hong Kong (China) and analyzes student-level questionnaire composite scores and scale scores. The manuscript reports a sample size of 6,037 students and describes standardization of variables, MCMC-based missing-data imputation, and then two-stage modeling (random forest followed by hierarchical linear modeling). However, it does not report whether PISA sampling weights or replicate weights were applied (e.g., no mention of W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT or BRR/jackknife). Because the primary predictive step uses random forest regression and the secondary step uses HLM, the paper’s weighting strategy is unclear; analysts should verify in the original PISA data documentation whether weights were used and, if not, interpret results as conditional on an unweighted analytic sample.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variables are well-being constructs measured via Likert-type questionnaire scales (positive affect, negative affect, life satisfaction, and meaning in life) rather than PISA cognitive achievement scores that are typically reported using PVs. The paper therefore does not require PV-based scaling/combining rules. Missing data handling is reported via MCMC-based imputation, so the main transparency issue is not PVs but whether survey weights were applied.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the PISA 2018 Hong Kong (China) dataset and analyzed 6,037 adolescents (mean age 15.73). The study selected 29 questionnaire-based background/composite variables and modeled four well-being outcomes (positive affect, negative affect, life satisfaction, meaning in life). Missing values were imputed using MCMC before analysis, and all variables were standardized (mean 0, SD 1). No additional grade- or school-type restriction is described beyond the reported grade distribution in the sample.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest regression with 10-fold cross-validation (5 repeats). Full 29 predictors explained 22.35% variance (MSE=0.78); final 7 predictors selected after cross-validation. Final model: school belonging contributed 84.97% mean decrease in %IncMSE; resilience contributed 48.74%IncMSE. HLM (top 7 predictors) RMSE=0.878; total variance explained=0.231; ICC=0.014.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Hong Kong (China) the study leveraged sense of belonging to school and resilience (plus additional school/teacher factors) to predict positive affect, finding that school belonging was the most salient predictor and resilience was the second most influential. This indicates that interventions strengthening students’ school connectedness and resilience may be effective levers for improving students’ day-to-day positive emotions, though the cross-sectional design prevents causal claims.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest regression with 10-fold cross-validation (5 repeats). Full 29 predictors explained 17.64% variance (MSE=0.82); final 7 predictors selected. Final model: general fear of failure contributed 57.13%IncMSE; school belonging contributed 31.38%IncMSE; other top variables contributed 5.42% to 21.33%. HLM (top 7 predictors) RMSE=0.893; total variance explained=0.205; ICC=0.025.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Hong Kong (China) the study leveraged general fear of failure and school belonging (along with resilience and school climate/bullying factors) to predict negative affect, finding that fear of failure was the top predictor and bullying-related and school-competition perceptions also mattered. This indicates that reducing evaluative pressure and fear of failure—while also addressing bullying and improving belonging—may help mitigate students’ negative emotions, though causality cannot be inferred from cross-sectional associations.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest regression with 10-fold cross-validation (5 repeats). Full 29 predictors explained 22.96% variance (MSE=0.77); final 7 predictors selected. HLM (top 7 predictors) RMSE=0.884; total variance explained=0.219; ICC=0.013. The paper reports that school belonging, parental support, resilience, teachers’ support, and interest were five salient predictors with %IncMSE ranging from 34.19 to 54.35; overall life satisfaction model R2=19.83% (RMSE=0.80) in the cross-validation step.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Hong Kong (China) the study leveraged school belonging, parental emotional support, and resilience (plus teacher support and teacher interest) to predict life satisfaction, finding that these family–school–individual factors jointly explained a substantial share of variance and that belonging and parental support were among the strongest contributors. This indicates that policies and school programs that enhance supportive parent–student relationships and students’ sense of belonging may improve global life satisfaction, while recognizing that the study’s cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest regression with 10-fold cross-validation (5 repeats). Full 29 predictors explained 27.05% variance (MSE=0.73); final 7 predictors selected. For eudaimonic well-being, top influential factors included resilience (ranked 1st) and work mastery (ranked 2nd) in the RF importance results; the paper reports %IncMSE ranges from 36.30 to 92.42 for selected factors. HLM (top 7 predictors) RMSE=0.846; total variance explained=0.287; ICC=0.012.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Hong Kong (China) the study leveraged resilience and mastery-related motivational factors (mastery goal orientation and work mastery) together with school belonging to predict meaning in life, finding that resilience was the most influential predictor and that mastery-oriented motivation strongly supported eudaimonic well-being. This indicates that educational interventions fostering adaptive coping and mastery goals—alongside strengthening belonging—may promote students’ sense of purpose, though the analysis cannot establish causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 Hong Kong (China) student questionnaire data (N=6,037) to predict four well-being outcomes: positive affect, negative affect, life satisfaction, and meaning in life (eudaimonic well-being). It first trains random forest regression models (10-fold cross-validation with 5 repeats) using 29 questionnaire-based composite predictors, selecting the top seven variables per outcome based on %IncMSE and RMSE. It then fits hierarchical linear models to estimate standardized effects while accounting for the nested student-within-school structure, reporting RMSE values around 0.846–0.893 and ICCs from 0.012 to 0.025. Key predictors differ by outcome: school belonging and resilience dominate positive affect and meaning in life, while fear of failure and bullying-related factors dominate negative affect. The paper imputes missing data via MCMC and standardizes variables, but it does not report whether PISA sampling/replicate weights were applied; additionally, cross-sectional PISA data prevent causal conclusions.
